title: Listening Under Pressure: The Riverside Archive Project
instructions: 本材料为模拟练习，非官方雅思试题，也不对应任何官方分数。阅读部分共三篇文章，总词数约2400词，请先通读文章再作答。听力部分共四个部分，每个部分10题，请先阅读题目再听录音（录音文字稿附后，实际练习时请先遮住文字稿）。所有填空题答案必须与原文完全一致，且不超过规定的词数。判断题只有三个选项：正确、错误、未提及。请仔细阅读每道题的解析和证据。

PASSAGE 1

A. The Riverside Community Archive began in 2019 as a modest attempt to preserve the memories of a small town in the north of England. Its founder, a retired librarian named Margaret Hollis, had spent thirty years cataloguing books and had grown increasingly concerned that the everyday voices of ordinary residents were disappearing. She placed an advertisement in the local newspaper asking people to bring in old photographs, letters, and diaries. The response was unexpected: within three months, more than four hundred items had been donated, ranging from a Victorian school register to a collection of cassette tapes recorded in the 1980s. The archive was initially housed in a single room in the town hall, but as the collection grew, it became clear that more space was needed. In 2021, the archive moved to its current premises above the town library.

B. The archive now occupies two rooms above the town library. One room is climate-controlled and holds the physical collection; the other serves as a listening booth where visitors can play digitised recordings. According to the current coordinator, Daniel Okafor, the most popular items are the oral history interviews conducted with residents who worked at the now-closed Riverside Mill. These interviews, recorded between 2015 and 2018, capture the daily routines, jokes, and complaints of factory life. Okafor notes that the mill employed over six hundred people at its peak in 1962, and that almost every family in the town had at least one relative who worked there. The mill finally closed in 1985, and many former workers still meet regularly at the archive to share memories.

C. The archive operates on a small annual budget of approximately £18,000, most of which comes from the town council and a local charitable trust. Volunteers handle almost all the work: cataloguing, digitisation, and staffing the listening booth. There are currently twenty-three active volunteers, the youngest being a seventeen-year-old student and the oldest an eighty-four-year-old former mill worker. Training sessions are held on the first Saturday of every month, and new volunteers are asked to commit to at least four hours per month. In addition to these volunteers, the archive employs one part-time administrator, who works ten hours a week and is responsible for financial records and correspondence.

D. One of the archive's most ambitious projects is the 'Listening Under Pressure' workshop, designed for adults who want to improve their ability to understand spoken English in real-life situations. The workshop uses genuine archive recordings—interviews, phone calls, and public announcements—to train participants in note-taking and accurate transcription. Participants learn to distinguish between similar-sounding numbers (such as fifteen and fifty), to recognise when a speaker corrects themselves, and to record names and dates with correct spelling and capitalisation. The workshop runs for six weeks and costs £45, with a reduced fee of £20 for students and unemployed people. Each session lasts two hours, and participants are encouraged to practise between sessions using online materials provided by the archive.

E. Feedback from participants has been largely positive. A local nurse, Priya Sharma, said that the workshop helped her take clearer notes during telephone consultations with patients. A taxi driver reported that he now writes down addresses more carefully after mishearing a street name. However, not all comments have been favourable. One participant complained that the recordings were too fast, while another felt that the sessions focused too much on numbers and not enough on everyday conversation. Okafor acknowledges these criticisms and says the workshop is revised each year based on feedback. He also notes that the workshop has a waiting list, which suggests that demand is high.

F. The archive faces several challenges. The building that houses it is old and requires frequent repairs; a leak in 2022 damaged several boxes of documents, though most were successfully dried and restored. More significantly, the archive relies heavily on a small group of dedicated volunteers, and Okafor worries about what will happen when they retire. He is currently seeking funding to employ a part-time assistant coordinator, a role that would provide continuity and allow the archive to expand its outreach to local schools. Without additional staff, he fears that the archive may have to reduce its opening hours.

G. Looking ahead, the archive plans to launch a digital portal in 2026, making its catalogue searchable online. This would allow researchers from other regions to access the collection without travelling to the town. However, Okafor stresses that digitisation is not a substitute for the physical archive. 'A photograph on a screen is not the same as holding the original in your hands,' he says. 'Our job is to keep both the objects and the stories alive.' The archive also hopes to collaborate with local schools to develop educational resources based on its collection.

PASSAGE 2

A. Every year, millions of students around the world take notes during lectures, yet research suggests that many of them record information inaccurately. A common problem is the mishearing of numbers: a student may write 'fifteen' when the lecturer said 'fifty', or 'thirteen' instead of 'thirty'. Such errors can have serious consequences, particularly in medical, legal, and financial contexts. In response, some universities have introduced listening and note-taking modules as part of their academic skills programmes. These modules are often optional, but in some institutions they have become compulsory for students in certain fields, such as medicine and law.

B. One such programme, at a university in the Netherlands, uses a combination of live dictation and recorded dialogues. Students listen to a conversation between a doctor and a patient, for example, and must record the patient's age, medication dosage, and appointment date. The exercise is marked not only on the accuracy of the information but also on spelling and capitalisation. According to the programme's designer, Dr. Elske Visser, the aim is to simulate the pressure of real professional communication. 'In a real consultation, you cannot pause the patient and ask them to repeat everything,' she explains. 'You have to develop strategies for checking and confirming what you have heard.' The programme is taught over eight weeks and includes both individual and group activities.

C. Visser's team has identified several common sources of error. The first is the confusion of similar-sounding numbers, especially in rapid speech. The second is the mishearing of names, which are often unfamiliar and may be spelled in unexpected ways. The third is the failure to notice self-corrections: a speaker might say 'the meeting is on Tuesday—no, sorry, Wednesday', and a careless listener will record only the first day mentioned. The fourth is the incorrect use of singular and plural forms, such as writing 'three box' instead of 'three boxes'. A fifth, less common but potentially serious, is the confusion of similar abbreviations, such as 'mg' (milligrams) and 'ml' (millilitres).

D. To address these issues, the programme teaches a range of techniques. Students are encouraged to use abbreviations and symbols, but only ones they can reliably interpret later. They are taught to repeat back key information to the speaker for confirmation, a technique known as 'closed-loop communication'. They also practise writing numbers in both figures and words, so that '15' and 'fifteen' reinforce each other. Finally, they are trained to review their notes immediately after a conversation, while the memory is still fresh. Visser emphasises that these techniques are not merely academic; they are used daily by professionals in high-stakes environments.

E. The results of a small-scale evaluation were encouraging. In a simulated consultation task, students who had completed the programme made 40 per cent fewer numerical errors than a control group. However, the evaluation also revealed that improvements in spelling and capitalisation were less pronounced. Visser suggests that this is because spelling requires long-term practice, whereas note-taking strategies can be learned relatively quickly. She recommends that students continue to practise transcription regularly, even after the programme ends. The evaluation involved 120 students and was conducted over two academic years.

F. Not everyone agrees that note-taking should be taught as a separate skill. Some educators argue that the focus on accuracy can make students anxious and distract them from understanding the overall message. They suggest that students should first learn to listen for gist, and only later worry about details. Visser responds that both skills are necessary and that they can be developed in parallel. 'Accuracy and understanding are not enemies,' she says. 'The best note-takers are the ones who can do both.' She also points out that in many professional contexts, such as healthcare, accuracy is a matter of safety.

G. The programme has now been adopted by three other universities, and Visser's team is developing an online version for students who cannot attend in person. The online version will include interactive exercises with immediate feedback, allowing learners to practise at their own pace. Visser hopes that this will make the training accessible to a wider audience, including professionals who need to improve their listening skills for work. The online version is expected to be available in 2025, and a pilot study will be conducted with a small group of students before its full release.

PASSAGE 3

A. The relationship between spelling and pronunciation in English is notoriously complex. Unlike languages such as Spanish or Italian, where letters correspond fairly consistently to sounds, English spelling preserves many historical forms that no longer reflect how words are spoken. The word 'knight', for example, retains the 'k' and 'gh' that were pronounced in Middle English but are silent today. For learners, this creates a double challenge: they must learn both the sound of a word and its written form, which may offer few clues. The same is true of many other words, such as 'through', 'though', and 'thought', which look similar but are pronounced differently.

B. One area where this complexity is particularly evident is in the plural forms of nouns. Most English nouns form the plural by adding -s or -es, but there are numerous exceptions. Some nouns change their vowel, such as 'man' to 'men' and 'tooth' to 'teeth'. Others remain unchanged, such as 'sheep' and 'deer'. A few retain foreign plurals, such as 'crisis' to 'crises' and 'phenomenon' to 'phenomena'. For adult learners, these irregularities can be frustrating, but they are also a source of interesting insights into the history of the language. For example, the plural 'children' is a double plural, combining an old plural ending with -en.

C. Numbers present a different set of difficulties. In English, the difference between 'fifteen' and 'fifty' lies not only in the vowel sound but also in the stress pattern: 'fifteen' is stressed on the second syllable, while 'fifty' is stressed on the first. Similarly, 'thirteen' and 'thirty' are distinguished by both vowel quality and stress. In rapid speech, these distinctions can be subtle, and context is often required to disambiguate. A listener who hears 'the meeting is at fifteen' may need to infer from context that the speaker means 'fifteen' (i.e., 3 p.m.) rather than 'fifty'. In some contexts, such as giving a phone number or a flight number, speakers often group digits to avoid confusion.

D. Capitalisation is another area where English has specific conventions. Proper nouns, including names of people, places, and organisations, are always capitalised. Days of the week and months of the year are also capitalised, unlike in some other languages. Titles such as 'Doctor' or 'Professor' are capitalised when used as part of a name (e.g., 'Doctor Smith'), but not when used generically (e.g., 'she is a doctor'). These rules may seem arbitrary, but they help readers to identify names and distinguish them from common nouns. In addition, the first word of a sentence is always capitalised, as is the pronoun 'I'.

E. For learners who need to record information accurately, whether in a lecture or a conversation, these features of English can be a significant obstacle. However, they can also be mastered with practice. One useful strategy is to keep a personal list of commonly misspelled words and irregular plurals, reviewing it regularly. Another is to practise transcribing short audio clips, checking the transcript against the original. Over time, learners develop an intuitive sense of what 'looks right' in English spelling, just as native speakers do. It is also helpful to read widely, as exposure to correct spelling reinforces memory.

F. Teachers can support this process by providing clear explanations and plenty of examples. Rather than simply correcting errors, they can help learners understand why a particular spelling or plural form is used. For instance, explaining that 'sheep' has an irregular plural because it is an old Germanic word can make the form easier to remember. Similarly, pointing out the stress difference between 'fifteen' and 'fifty' can help learners both to hear and to produce the distinction. Teachers can also use minimal pairs—words that differ by only one sound—to practise listening discrimination.

G. Ultimately, the goal is not perfect accuracy but effective communication. A learner who writes 'three box' instead of 'three boxes' will still be understood, but a learner who mishears 'fifteen' as 'fifty' in a medical context could cause serious harm. By focusing on the areas of highest risk, learners can prioritise their efforts and achieve practical competence in listening and recording information. In an increasingly globalised world, the ability to listen accurately and record information correctly is a valuable skill in almost every profession.

SECTION 1: Social Dialogue

Man: Good morning. I'd like to book a place on the 'Listening Under Pressure' workshop, please.
Woman: Certainly. Can I take your name first?
Man: Yes, it's Daniel—no, sorry, it's David. David Chen.
Woman: Thank you, Mr Chen. And how did you hear about the workshop?
Man: A friend recommended it. She said it helped her a lot with phone calls at work.
Woman: Good. The next course starts on the fourth of March. That's a Tuesday. Does that suit you?
Man: The fourth of March... yes, that's fine. How much is it?
Woman: It's forty-five pounds, but if you're a student or unemployed, it's twenty pounds.
Man: I'm not a student, so I'll pay the full fee. Can I pay by card?
Woman: Yes, of course. And could I have a contact number?
Man: It's 07700 900 123. Sorry, let me repeat that: 07700 900 123.
Woman: Thank you. We'll send you a confirmation email. What's your email address?
Man: It's david.chen@email.com—all lowercase.
Woman: Got it. One more thing: the workshop runs for six weeks, every Tuesday from 6 to 8 p.m. Is that okay?
Man: Yes, that's perfect. Thank you very much.

SECTION 2: Social Monologue

Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Riverside Community Archive. My name is Margaret Hollis, and I'm the founder. Before we start, I'd like to give you a quick introduction to what we do here. The archive was started in 2019, and we now have over four hundred items in our collection. These include photographs, letters, diaries, and audio recordings. Our most popular collection is the oral history interviews with former workers from the Riverside Mill. The mill closed in 1985, but at its peak in 1962 it employed over six hundred people. We're always looking for volunteers. At the moment we have twenty-three active volunteers, and we hold training sessions on the first Saturday of every month. If you're interested, please speak to me or to Daniel Okafor, our coordinator. Finally, I'd like to mention our workshop, 'Listening Under Pressure', which starts on the fourth of March. It's designed for adults who want to improve their listening and note-taking skills. Thank you for listening.

SECTION 3: Academic Discussion

Tutor: So, Emma, you've been looking at the evaluation of the note-taking programme. What did you find?
Student: Well, the results were quite positive overall. Students who completed the programme made forty per cent fewer numerical errors than the control group.
Tutor: Forty per cent—that's impressive. What about spelling and capitalisation?
Student: That's the interesting part. The improvements there were much smaller. Dr Visser thinks it's because spelling takes longer to learn.
Tutor: That makes sense. Did the evaluation look at anything else?
Student: Yes, they also asked students about their anxiety levels. Some students said they felt more anxious when they focused on accuracy.
Tutor: Hmm. So there's a tension between accuracy and fluency.
Student: Exactly. But Visser argues that you can develop both at the same time. She says accuracy and understanding are not enemies.
Tutor: I see. And what about the online version?
Student: They're developing it now. It'll have interactive exercises with immediate feedback. It should be available next year.
Tutor: Good. So for your essay, you could compare the face-to-face and online versions.
Student: Yes, that's what I was thinking.

SECTION 4: Academic Lecture

Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about the challenges of transcribing spoken English, particularly for learners. There are four common sources of error that I'd like to discuss. First, similar-sounding numbers. In English, 'fifteen' and 'fifty' are distinguished by both vowel sound and stress. 'Fifteen' is stressed on the second syllable, while 'fifty' is stressed on the first. In rapid speech, this distinction can be hard to hear. Second, names. Names are often unfamiliar and may be spelled in unexpected ways. A name like 'Siobhan', for example, is pronounced 'Shivon'. Third, self-corrections. Speakers often correct themselves mid-sentence, saying things like 'the meeting is on Tuesday—no, Wednesday'. A careless listener may record only the first day. Fourth, singular and plural forms. Learners may write 'three box' instead of 'three boxes'. To address these issues, I recommend three strategies. One: use abbreviations and symbols, but only ones you can interpret later. Two: repeat back key information for confirmation. Three: review your notes immediately after the conversation. Research suggests that these strategies can significantly reduce errors. Thank you.

grammar.title: 名词单复数、拼写、数字和大小写；问句结构复查
